# AI Disclosure Labels

A WordPress plugin. Mark an image as generated by AI, or as a real image modified using AI, and a disclosure label appears everywhere that image is shown.

Built because the EU AI Act (Article 50) has applied since 2 August 2026 and adding a caption by hand is something you forget on the fifth post.

## What it does

The mark lives on the **attachment**, not on the post, so marking a file once covers every place it is reused.

* A *Generated by AI* / *Modified using AI* picker in the Media Library and in the media modal.
* An *AI disclosure* panel next to the featured image in the block editor, saved straight to the attachment over REST.
* An *AI* column in the media library list view.
* On the front end: a caption under large images, a compact badge on thumbnails — or a position and style you pick yourself.
* Settings for label text per kind, position (under the image or any of its four corners), style (plain, dark, white, translucent), size, opacity, and where to show it.
* Uninstall removes the settings and every mark.

## Where the labels come from

Four entry points, all going through one scan with the same guards:

| Hook | Covers |
|---|---|
| `post_thumbnail_html` | featured images |
| `wp_get_attachment_image` | anything a theme renders with the standard function |
| `the_content` | content images, classic editor included |
| `render_block` | core image, gallery and media-and-text blocks |

Images a theme prints itself — `<img src="<?php echo $field['url']; ?>">` straight out of an ACF field — pass through no filter at all. For those there is an optional pass over the finished page: the plugin already knows which attachments are marked, so it builds a file-name list for those few files only, caches it, and looks for exactly those names. No query per image, and matching on the file name survives a CDN or an offloaded upload path.

Or call it from the template yourself:

```php
<?php aidl_label( $attachment_id ); ?>
```

```
[ai_disclosure id="123"]
```

## Filters

```php
apply_filters( 'aidl_label_text', $text, $attachment_id, $variant, $mode );
apply_filters( 'aidl_badge_text', $text, $attachment_id, $mode );
```

## Layout

```
ai-disclosure-labels.php   plugin header, constants, mode helpers
includes/media.php         marking: meta, media fields, editor assets
includes/frontend.php      labels on the front end
includes/catch-all.php     optional pass over the finished page
includes/settings.php      Settings -> AI Disclosure Labels
assets/editor.js           block editor panel, no JSX and no build step
languages/                 .pot, pl_PL .po/.mo and the JSON for wp.i18n
tools/build-lang.php       regenerates everything in languages/
tools/tests.php            label logic against WordPress stubs
uninstall.php              removes settings and marks
```

No build step, no external requests, no database tables.

## Development

```bash
php -l ai-disclosure-labels.php && for f in includes/*.php; do php -l "$f"; done
cd tools && php tests.php        # 30 checks on the label logic
cd tools && php build-lang.php   # after changing any translatable string
```

`tools/tests.php` stubs the handful of WordPress functions the label logic touches, so it runs anywhere PHP does. It covers the cases that actually broke something: a theme returning a whole `<figure>` for the featured image, a 150px thumbnail getting a full caption, `<picture>` from a WebP converter, a fragment coming back from a cache without the marker, and the two modes.

## Releasing

`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` pushes a tag to the WordPress.org SVN repository. Set `SVN_USERNAME` and `SVN_PASSWORD` in the repository secrets, then:

```bash
git tag 1.2.0 && git push --tags
```

`.distignore` keeps `tools/`, tests and repository metadata out of the shipped plugin.

## History

The first version was a prototype for one site (`wd-oznaczenia-ai`, first commit here). It was then rewritten for the plugin directory as `ai-disclosure-labels`, and went through 1.0.0, 1.0.1 and 1.1.0 in one evening before this repository existed — those were never released and their intermediate file states were not kept, so the second commit is 1.2.0. `readme.txt` carries the changelog.
